routing queue, anticipate institutional order flow, and extract microscopic rents from traditional

In January 2015, the SEC formally charged the exchanges with violating Sections 19(b) and 
19(g) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (Case Number 3-16332).1 To settle the charges, 
Direct Edge and Bats Global Markets agreed to pay a $14 million financial penalty, representing 
the largest-ever penalty levied against a financial exchange at that time.1 
Due Diligence Implications of the Lehman Tenure 
It is imperative to note that Michael Bleich was not personally named as a defendant or 
respondent in the SEC’s enforcement action against BATS and Direct Edge.1 However, from a 
strict operational due diligence perspective, his proximity to this scandal is a highly relevant 
qualitative data point.1 As the Head of Liquidity Strategy, Bleich aggressively championed and 
integrated Lehman Brothers into a trading venue that was structurally designed to facilitate 
predatory high-frequency trading at the explicit expense of market transparency and fair 
execution.1 
The BATS scandal perfectly illustrates the environment in which Bleich honed his strategies—a 
marketplace characterized by extreme speed, dark liquidity, selective disclosure, and 
regulatory arbitrage.1 When this professional background is combined with his subsequent 
proprietary trading actions, a distinct, deeply concerning behavioral pattern emerges, 
establishing the exact psychological and operational framework that Bleich would later deploy 
against Arnulf Damerau.1 
3. The Apex of Financial Misconduct: Scout Trading, 
LLC and Systemic Regulation SHO Violations 
Following the collapse of Lehman Brothers, Bleich transitioned from an institutional bank 
executive to an independent proprietary trading entrepreneur.1 In May 2009, he founded Scout 
Trading, LLC, a Delaware-domiciled proprietary trading firm headquartered at 120 West 45th 
Street in New York City.1 Operating as a FINRA-registered broker-dealer (CRD No. 151990) and 
a registered member of the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE), Scout Trading 
represented the unfettered application of Bleich’s expertise in quantitative liquidity strategies.1 
The absolute apex of Michael Bleich’s regulatory exposure is the joint enforcement action 
brought by The NASDAQ Stock Market LLC and FINRA against Scout Trading.1 Bleich served as
